planting.note: Also plants well in early fall; give it well-drained soil and let it establish before the first hard freeze.

directions: Buddy is a cross between common boxwood and Korean boxwood, named for Buddy Hubbuch, the late curator of Bernheim Arboretum and Research Forest who selected it. It builds a slightly wide-spreading rounded mound of large, glossy dark-green leaves at a slow pace of just a couple inches a year, so it holds a tidy shape with little shearing. It handles full sun to partial shade and shrugs off deer and leafminer, though like most heirloom-type boxwood it has no special resistance to boxwood blight, so give it airy spacing and good drainage.

planting.note: Spring planting also works; mulch new plants to even out soil moisture through their first winter.

directions: Cranberry Creek was introduced by Willoway Nurseries in Ohio for its reddish-bronze, cranberry-colored flush of new growth, which settles into a deep, glossy green as the season progresses. It naturally tightens into a dense, broad pyramid, so it needs only light touch-up shearing to stay formal. It takes full sun best but still performs in partial shade, tolerates deer pressure, and is a good scaled-down choice for foundation plantings or container specimens where a classic boxwood silhouette is wanted without decades of growing time.

planting.note: Prune lightly right after planting and again in late winter to encourage a denser mound.

directions: This dwarf Korean selection pushes lime-green new growth each spring that darkens over summer and takes on bronze winter tones, giving it a noticeably stronger seasonal color shift than most English or American boxwood. It grows into a low, dense mound rather than up, making it a natural fit for edging beds or a low formal hedge. Growers note it carries more natural tolerance of boxwood leafminer than older heirloom cultivars, though it still benefits from good air circulation and well-drained soil.

planting.note: Fall planting is also fine in milder zones; keep new plants watered through their first dry season.

directions: Little Mister (US Plant Patent 36,215) is a patented littleleaf boxwood bred as roughly twice the size of the popular dwarf Little Missy, while keeping the same dense, dark-green habit. It takes shaping easily for small hedges or container topiary and holds its color well through winter. Once established it tolerates short dry spells better than many older boxwood cultivars, making it a lower-maintenance option where a larger-scale dwarf form is wanted.

planting.note: Site it where its narrow mature width will still read as a vertical accent, not a hedge.

directions: Green Pillar is a boxwood selection grown for a naturally narrow, columnar habit, climbing into a tall, slender green column that stays narrow even if it is never trimmed. Growth is slow to moderate rather than fast, so it takes some years to build real height, but because its lateral spread is so limited by nature it needs very little pruning to keep a crisp formal line. It is a useful way to build a vertical accent or a narrow privacy screen without the width a sheared sempervirens hedge would eventually need.

planting.note: Give it rich, moist, well-drained soil to sustain its unusually fast vertical growth rate.

directions: Sky Walker (US Plant Patent 22,977, bred by West Oregon Nursery) is marketed as the fastest-growing boxwood available, adding as much as two and a half feet of height in a single season on its way to becoming a tall, narrow living column. It develops very few lateral side branches, so the dense, upright form stays tight without much shaping. Because of its rapid rise and modest width, it suits tall screening or vertical topiary accents far better than it suits a clipped low hedge.

planting.note: Fall planting works too; its vigorous root system establishes readily even in lean soils.

directions: Babylon Beauty is one of four releases in the European Better Boxwood program (PP32,273), a two-decade breeding effort aimed squarely at boxwood blight resistance, and unlike its more upright siblings in the same collection it naturally grows wider than it is tall. The light green, fine-textured foliage and spreading habit make it read more like a groundcover than a hedge plant unless it is pruned upward. Its breeders selected for a notably vigorous, sturdy root system, so it tolerates poorer or sandier soils better than many classic boxwood selections once it is established.
sources: Better Boxwood (Plant Development Services / Concept Plants)
